title: Extraoral imaging: DPT, ceph & CBCT
blurb: Panoramic (DPT/OPG), lateral cephalometric and CBCT imaging: what each shows, how the patient is prepared, and what each can't do.
question: A 19-year-old is referred for a panoramic radiograph to assess his lower wisdom teeth. While you prepare him, he asks whether this one big X-ray means he won't need any more 'small ones' for decay. What do you need to do to prepare him, and how should his question be answered?

teach.body: Extraoral imaging places the receptor outside the mouth, so it can cover a much larger area than an intraoral film. The three you'll meet are the dental panoramic tomograph (DPT, also called an OPG or orthopantomogram), the lateral cephalometric radiograph (lateral ceph) used in orthodontics, and cone beam computed tomography (CBCT), which builds a three-dimensional image. Each has its own uses, limits and dose, and each needs careful patient preparation to avoid a retake.

teach.caption: Both jaws and every tooth on one image, along with the maxillary sinuses, nasal area and the rami of the mandible. The tubehead and receptor rotate around the patient's head during the exposure.

teach.h: DPT: good for, not good for

rows.label: Overview of both jaws and the developing dentition
Fractures of the mandible, large cysts or lesions
Detailed apical infection or root fine detail

teach.note: A DPT has less fine detail than intraoral images and includes distortion, magnification and 'ghost' shadows, so it cannot replace bitewings or periapicals.

teach.h: Preparing a patient for a DPT

steps.label: Bite on the peg
steps.sub: Front teeth in the groove of the bite block

steps.label: Tongue to the palate
steps.sub: Lips closed around the bite block

teach.caption: Each step prevents a specific fault: metal leaves white artefacts, movement causes blurring, and a tongue left down leaves a dark band over the upper tooth roots.
The skull in profile, showing how the upper and lower jaws relate to each other and to the skull base, the angle of the incisors, and the soft-tissue profile of the nose, lips and chin.

teach.body: For a lateral ceph the head is held in a cephalostat, with ear rods in the ear canals, the Frankfort plane horizontal, teeth together and lips relaxed. Orthodontists use it to assess skeletal jaw relationships, incisor inclination and the soft-tissue profile, and to plan and monitor treatment. CBCT produces a 3D image. It is used when 2D views aren't enough, for example implant planning, or checking how close a wisdom tooth is to the mandibular canal. It carries a higher dose and needs extra training to justify and report.

teach.caption: For CBCT the whole room is the controlled area because it produces more scattered radiation.
Bars show the top of each published range (FGDP/CGDent Selection Criteria, 2018). A DPT is no more than about 6 days of natural background radiation.

teach.text: A DPT is a broad overview, not a 'super X-ray'. It does NOT replace bitewings for early caries or periapicals for apical infection, and a ceph does NOT replace a periapical either.

items: DPT/OPG: both jaws on one image, tubehead and receptor rotate around the head; great for third molars.
DPT limits: less detail, distortion and ghost shadows; not for early caries or apical detail.
Lateral ceph: skull in profile in a cephalostat with ear rods; orthodontic jaw and incisor relationships.
CBCT: 3D, highest dose, used only when 2D imaging isn't enough; whole room is the controlled area.

summary: You can now describe the DPT, lateral ceph and CBCT, say what each is used for and what it can't show, prepare a patient for a panoramic radiograph step by step, and put their doses in context.

A.q: Which radiograph is most suitable for assessing impacted lower third molars and the surrounding jaw?
A.why: A DPT shows both jaws including the third molar regions and rami, making it the standard view for impacted wisdom teeth.

whyNot.0: Bitewings show posterior crowns only, not the whole third molar and its roots.
whyNot.2: An upper occlusal shows the anterior maxilla.
whyNot.3: A lateral ceph shows skeletal relationships in profile, with the two sides superimposed.

A.q: A student says a DPT can replace bitewings for detecting early decay between teeth. What is the best response?
options: Correct, it gives a higher dose
Incorrect, it only shows one jaw
A.why: A DPT has less fine detail and some distortion, so it can't reliably detect early interproximal caries; bitewings are needed.

whyNot.0: Showing every tooth isn't the same as showing enough detail for early caries.
whyNot.1: A higher dose doesn't mean better detail, and that wouldn't justify replacing bitewings.
whyNot.3: A DPT shows both jaws, so that isn't the reason.

A.q: Before a panoramic radiograph, why must the patient remove earrings and piercings?
A.why: Metal objects absorb X-rays and appear as white (radiopaque) artefacts that can hide anatomy.

whyNot.1: Jewellery doesn't raise the patient's dose; the issue is image quality.
whyNot.2: The machine doesn't detect jewellery or stop because of it.
whyNot.3: Metal shows as white, not dark, and only where it lies.

B.q: An orthodontist needs to assess the skeletal relationship of the jaws and incisor inclination. Which radiograph is requested?
B.why: A lateral ceph shows the skull in profile, so jaw relationships, incisor angles and soft-tissue profile can be measured.

whyNot.0: A periapical shows one or two teeth, not skeletal relationships.
whyNot.1: A lower occlusal shows the floor of the mouth and lower arch.
whyNot.3: A vertical bitewing shows posterior bone levels.

B.q: During a DPT, what should the patient do with their tongue?
options: Let it rest on the floor of the mouth
Push it against the lower teeth
Stick it out over the bite peg
Press it flat against the palate
B.why: With the tongue against the palate, the air space above it is removed, so the roots of the upper teeth aren't obscured.

whyNot.0: A tongue resting low leaves an air gap that shows as a dark band over the upper roots.
whyNot.1: Pushing it against the lower teeth still leaves an air space under the palate.
whyNot.2: Sticking the tongue out would move the head and spoil positioning.

B.q: During a lateral ceph, what holds the patient's head in position?
B.why: A cephalostat uses ear rods in the external ear canals to hold the head in a fixed, reproducible position.

whyNot.1: A bite block is used for a DPT; ceph positioning relies on ear rods.
whyNot.2: Staff must never hold patients during an exposure.
whyNot.3: A thyroid collar is protection, used only if indicated, and doesn't position the head.

C.q: Which statement about dental CBCT is correct?
options: It replaces bitewings for routine checks
It gives the lowest dental dose
C.why: CBCT builds a three-dimensional image and is used only when 2D imaging isn't enough.

whyNot.0: CBCT is not a routine caries screening tool.
whyNot.1: CBCT has the highest dose range of dental imaging (about 11–214 µSv small field).
whyNot.2: Dentists need additional training to justify and report CBCT.

C.q: What happens to the tubehead and receptor during a panoramic exposure?
options: The tubehead goes in the mouth
C.why: In panoramic imaging the tubehead and receptor rotate around the patient's head to create one image of both jaws.

whyNot.0: A stationary set-up would not create a panoramic image.
whyNot.2: No part of the tubehead goes inside the mouth.
whyNot.3: Both components move together in opposite positions around the head.

C.q: Why is the whole room designated as the controlled area for dental CBCT?
C.why: CBCT generally produces higher levels of scattered radiation, so the whole room (option A) is the recommended controlled area.

whyNot.1: CBCT is digital and doesn't need a darkroom.
whyNot.2: Patient position isn't the reason for the controlled area designation.
whyNot.3: CBCT uses digital detectors, not film.

reteach.title: Map, profile photo and 3D model
reteach.question: If you were showing someone a town, when would you use a road map, a side-on photo, or a 3D model?

blocks.body: A DPT is the road map: the whole area at once, perfect for finding where things are (like a buried wisdom tooth), but you can't read the house numbers, so small decay is missed. A lateral ceph is the side-on photo of the skyline: it shows how big structures line up, which is what an orthodontist needs. CBCT is the 3D model: it shows depth and exactly what sits next to what, but it's costly in dose, so it's only used when the map and photo can't answer the question.

Answers
rows: How do the jaws line up?

blocks.text: The bigger the picture, the less fine detail. That's why bitewings and periapicals are still needed after a DPT.

explain.body: Tubehead and receptor rotate around the head, giving both jaws on one image. Best for third molars, jaw overviews, fractures and large lesions. Less detail, plus distortion and ghost shadows.

explain.caption: A panoramic radiograph: both jaws in one view.

test.q: Which is a recognised LIMITATION of a panoramic radiograph?
test.why: Panoramic images have lower fine detail and some distortion compared with intraoral radiographs.

whyNot.0: Third molars are one of the main reasons for taking a DPT.
whyNot.2: A DPT shows both jaws, not a single quadrant.
whyNot.3: The maxillary sinuses are visible on a DPT.

explain.body: Remove metal items, stand straight, bite in the groove of the peg, Frankfort plane horizontal, tongue on the palate, lips closed, and stay still. Each step prevents a known fault.

test.q: A patient moves during a DPT exposure. What is the most likely result?
options: A dark band over the upper roots
test.why: Movement during the rotation smears the image, producing blurring or distortion.

whyNot.1: A dark band over upper roots comes from the tongue not touching the palate.
whyNot.2: White artefacts are caused by metal objects left in place.
whyNot.3: A blank image suggests an equipment or processing failure, not movement.

explain.body: The skull in profile, held in a cephalostat with ear rods, teeth together and lips relaxed. Used for orthodontic and jaw surgery planning: skeletal relationships, incisor inclination and soft-tissue profile.

explain.caption: A lateral ceph: jaws, incisors and soft-tissue profile.

test.q: A lateral ceph is most useful for which purpose?
test.why: A lateral ceph shows skeletal and dental relationships in profile, which orthodontists use to plan treatment.

whyNot.3: Submandibular stones need a lower true occlusal.

explain.body: Cone beam CT makes a 3D image of a selected area. Used when 2D views can't answer the question: implant planning, a wisdom tooth close to the mandibular canal, impacted canines. Highest dental dose; whole room is the controlled area.

test.q: When is a CBCT scan most likely to be justified?
options: When 2D images can't answer the question
test.why: Because of its higher dose, CBCT is only justified when conventional 2D imaging is inadequate for the clinical question.

whyNot.0: Routine scans without a clinical question are never justified.
whyNot.1: CBCT is not a substitute for bitewings, especially in more radiosensitive children.
whyNot.3: Patient request alone does not justify an exposure.
